title: Motion for Reply and Reply of American Transmission Company LLC to Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.'s 10/09/2026 Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer under ER26-3531.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


American Transmission Company LLC                                      Docket No. ER26-3531-000


                           MOTION FOR REPLY AND REPLY OF
                         AMERICAN TRANSMISSION COMPANY LLC

          Pursuant to Sections 212 and 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1

American Transmission Company LLC (ATC) by its corporate manager, ATC Management Inc.

(collectively, ATC) hereby files this Motion for Leave to Reply and Reply to the Motion for

Leave to Answer and Answer of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO)

filed on October 9, 2026. On August 17, 2026, ATC filed its proposed revisions to Attachment

FF-ATCLLC of MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets

Tariff (Tariff) in response to the Commission’s Show Cause Order. 2 ATC’s proposed revisions

address the immediate need for large load integration in the ATC service territory and are just

and reasonable and should be accepted without hearing or settlement proceedings with an

effective date of October 17, 2026.

          MISO does not dispute that ATC’s local planning has functioned successfully without

issue for two decades or that differences within the region are commonplace, and MISO provides

no evidence that ATC’s proposal will cause harm. Instead, MISO avers that ATC’s proposal may

differ from MISO’s processes at some point in the future that may create implementation and




1
    18 C.F.R. § 385.212-213 (2026).
2
 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal
Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”).
 reliability challenges. 3 ATC appreciates MISO's recognition that immediate implementation of

Attachment FF-ATCLLC addresses an important near-term need. Approval of Attachment FF-

ATCLLC should not be temporary or conditioned on future filings; however, ATC remains

committed to working with MISO through the stakeholder process and evaluating any future

Commission-approved requirements to determine whether further modifications are warranted.

The issue before the Commission in this proceeding is whether ATC's proposed Attachment FF-

ATCLLC is just and reasonable, not whether a future MISO proposal might ultimately be

preferred.

I.       REPLY

         A.      FPA Section 205 Requires that the Commission Accept ATC’s Proposal if It is
                 Just and Reasonable.

         In this Section 205 proceeding, the Commission must evaluate whether ATC’s proposed

changes to its Attachment FF-ATCLLC are just and reasonable. It is not a question whether

there are other just and reasonable alternatives or whether other parties suggest that there are

changes to the proposal that they would prefer. 4 ATC’s proposed changes to Attachment FF-

proposals raised by intervenors because proposed reforms were just and reasonable); Entergy Svcs., Inc. v.
FERC, 40 F.4th 689, 701–02 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (finding that the Commission is not required to choose the
best solution, only a reasonable one.); Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 128 FERC ¶ 61,265, at P 21
(2009) (“Under the [FPA], the issue before the Commission is whether the [independent system
operator’s] proposal is just and reasonable and not whether the proposal is more or less reasonable than
other alternatives.”); Southwest Power Pool, Inc., 193 FERC ¶ 61,198 (2025) (Accreditation methodology
need not predict the future with perfect accuracy, rather the filing party need only show that the proposed
methodology would be sufficiently accurate so as to produce just and reasonable results.); Petal Gas
Storage, L.L.C. v. FERC, 496 F.3d 695, 703 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (“[The Commission] is not required to
choose the best solution, only a reasonable one.”); See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 169 FERC ¶ 61,038,
at P 12 (2019) (citing OXY USA, Inc. v. FERC, 64 F.3d 679, 692 (D.C. Cir. 1995) (finding that under the

not be the only reasonable methodology, or even the most accurate one”)); Cities of Bethany v. FERC, 727
F.2d 1131, 1136 (D.C. Cir. 1984) (when determining whether a rate was just and reasonable, the
                                                    2
 ATCLLC are just and reasonable because they (1) provide an immediately implementable path

forward for integrating large loads, consistent with ATC’s current practices and responsive to the

requirements in the Show Cause Order, (2) provide certainty for large-load projects already

underway in ATC’s footprint, (3) contain urgently needed protections against cost shifting among

wholesale customers, and (4) align with Public Service Commission of Wisconsin retail tariff

requirements.

           MISO agrees that its Show Cause Order compliance processes are working their way

through the stakeholder process and could take many months to be final. Yet MISO asserts that

ATC’s Attachment FF-ATCLLC may be problematic at some point in the future. For example,

MISO asks the Commission to allow ATC’s proposed requirements only where MISO has no

corresponding requirements, 5 but MISO has no corresponding requirements that are effective to

date. Even if MISO develops corresponding requirements in the future, MISO only speculates

that ATC’s requirements will cause harm. 6 Alternatively, MISO asks the Commission to allow

ATC to impose stricter requirements in cases where MISO has an established framework. 7

Again, there is no established framework and any conjecture as to what might be stricter is

unknown. 8 The Commission should not judge ATC’s Attachment FF-ATCLLC planning

framework based on MISO’s speculation that ATC’s proposal may conflict with MISO’s

processes in the future and that such conflict will cause harm. If a future conflict arises that may

cause harm, it can be addressed at that time.


Commission properly did not consider “whether a proposed rate schedule is more or less reasonable than
alternative rate designs”).
5
    MISO Answer at 2.
6
    Id. at 4 (suggesting that ATC’s proposal “ultimately could create a less stringent standard.”).
7
    Id. at 2.
8
    Id. at 4 (asserting that ATC’s framework “could result in ambiguity and uncertainty”).

                                                        3
            Thus, for purposes of Section 205 approval of ATC’s filing, MISO has not presented an

alternative proposal that the Commission could consider. A speculative future conflict does not

justify delaying ATC’s requested October 17, 2026 effective date for revisions that are

independently just and reasonable and responsive to the Show Cause Order.

           B.     Conditioning ATC’s Proposed Changes to Attachment FF-ATCLLC on
                  Compliance with Yet-Unknown Uniform Base-Level Rules Without a
                  Demonstrable Need Will Impose Unnecessary Costs in ATC’s Footprint and
                  Undermine Policy Goals to Advance AI.

           MISO argues that uniform base-level rules are needed to address reliability concerns and

that if ATC had different standards, it would create operational risk. 9 MISO has asserted

potential reliability concerns but has not demonstrated any specific reliability deficiency,

operational limitation, or planning concern that would result from ATC's proposed framework.

From a planning standpoint, there has been and will continue to be significant coordination

between ATC and MISO regarding the planning of the system. Indeed, all of ATC’s projects

must be evaluated in MISO’s regional MTEP process—either through the regular planning cycle

or through the Expedited Project Review (EPR) process. 10 That will not change.

           From an operations standpoint, it should be abundantly clear that ATC's proposal does

not prevent MISO from obtaining information necessary to maintain reliable system

operations. ATC is not proposing to displace otherwise applicable MISO requirements

governing load forecasting, telemetry, real-time information, or operational visibility. 11 The



9
    Id. at 4.
10
     ATC Answer at 2, 9.
11
  ATC’s proposed changes to Attachment FF-ATCLLC include language requiring ATC to “maintain
additional data monitoring, data retention, forecasting and design criteria in applicable ATCLLC Business
Practices.” ATC Transmittal Letter, Tab A, Redlined Attachment FF-ATCLLC, Section V.E. While ATC
maintains its own visibility requirements necessary for its operations, ATC’s requirements will not impact
MISO’s load forecasting, telemetry, real-time information, or operational visibility requirements.

                                                    4
 material differences addressed by Attachment FF-ATCLLC concern ATC’s local planning, study,

interconnection, and cost-allocation framework that are part of ATC’s local planning role, for

which ATC has developed study-based criteria tailored to its system. Attachment FF-ATCLLC

will not affect MISO’s ability to obtain the operational information needed to operate the

regional system.

        Attachment FF-ATCLLC was adopted to fulfill ATC’s state law mandate. Under the

Wisconsin law that enabled ATC to be formed, ATC is not permitted to delegate its planning

obligations under state law to any other entity. 12 Since the initial approval of Attachment FF-

ATCLLC, the Commission has approved ATC’s proposed changes to comply with other major

planning orders without concern for operational risks. In compliance with Order Nos. 890, 13 and

1000, 14 the Commission approved (and MISO did not object) to ATC being the only transmission

owner in the MISO footprint at that time to decline to integrate its local planning functions into

MISO’s Attachment FF. 15

(emphasis added).

         Contrary to MISO’s claims, Attachment FF-ATCLLC does not exceed the traditional

bounds of ATC’s local planning criteria. Large loads are retail customers of the local distribution

companies in ATC’s footprint. ATC’s planning for large loads interconnecting with the local

distribution companies on ATC’s system is fundamental to ATC’s local planning function and

will impact retail electric service in ATC’s footprint for many years to come. Delegating that

function to MISO is contrary to Wisconsin law and prior Commission orders, and would subvert

ATC’s obligations to its stakeholders.

        Moreover, contrary to MISO’s claims, ATC has adequately addressed cost allocation in

Attachment FF-ATCLLC to comply with state retail tariff requirements. Differences in cost

allocation policies have not been problematic in the past. In the generation interconnection

context, ATC has had different network upgrade cost allocation provisions from the rest of the

MISO region with no negative impacts. 16

        MISO’s alleged harm is based on conjecture and dependent on tariff provisions that have

not yet been filed or accepted by the Commission. ATC’s amendments to Attachment FF-

ATCLLC are supported by studies used in developing the planning criteria to address the needs

of its system and will apply to large loads in its footprint. 17 We are not aware of any similar



et.al., 132 FERC ¶ 61,119 at P 22 (2010) (order accepting compliance filing and noting that ATC’s
projects still must flow through MTEP.).
16
  For several years, ATC had a roll-in cost allocation policy for generator interconnection network
upgrades when MISO had adopted a participant funding methodology. American Transmission Co. LLC,
120 FERC ¶ 61,221 at P 17 (2007)(“We likewise find that the proposal of ATC to adopt a 100%
reimbursement policy is just and reasonable. As long-recognized by the courts, different rate proposals
can be just and reasonable; there is no one correct method for calculating rates.”) order denying reh’g,
123 FERC ¶ 61,065 (2008).
17
  ATC engaged specialized power system consultants to study large loads, including flicker analyses,
rotor-swing modes, generator-shaft studies to develop ramp-rate, and voltage-ride-through requirements.
ATC Answer at 7. The proposed changes to Attachment FF-ATCLLC’s operating requirements are based
on these extensive studies and advance these proven large load processes developed over the past several
years.

                                                   6
 studies by MISO. MISO is assuming that its requirements will be more stringent than ATC’s but

that remains unknown. ATC’s studies were intended to build efficiencies in design, maintain safe

and reliable service, and rein in costs. Any perceived need for more stringent planning/operating

requirements is not supported by studies. Without additional technical support, uniformity for

the sake of uniformity will add an unnecessary burden to large load customers in ATC’s footprint

by requiring unnecessary and costly equipment requirements. This poses the risk of driving up

costs for customers and undermining the administration’s policy goals for advancing AI (or super

intelligence).

        ATC has already committed to adjusting its processes, if necessary, as MISO’s

requirements develop through the stakeholder process. It is unreasonable for MISO to suggest

that ATC should defer or condition its proposal because it may conflict with MISO’s future Show

Cause Order compliance filing.

          C.     The Commission has Encouraged Individual Transmission Owners to Make
                 Section 205 Filings to Address the Show Cause Order Requirements and to
                 Facilitate AI Development.

        As the Commission noted in the Show Cause Order, ATC’s current Attachment FF-

ATCLLC includes an approved distribution-to-transmission interconnection process and a load

interconnection procedure, but it does not have procedures specific to large loads. 18 ATC is

following the Commission’s directive in the Show Cause Order with proposed revisions in this

filing that are intended to fill that gap and to be tailored to work within the established

Attachment FF-ATCLLC procedures. The Commission has encouraged transmission owners to




18
   Show Cause Order at n. 75. The Commission recognized that ATC has established procedures for
interconnection of large loads outside of the Tariff. Id. at P 21, n. 77.

                                                  7
 propose tariff revisions to address issues pursuant to their applicable Section 205 filing rights. 19

ATC’s proposal here is intended to comply with the Show Cause Order and formalize what ATC

is already doing in its footprint to manage the challenges of large load integration and facilitate

AI development, as well as adopt new practices required of the Show Cause Order. 20

II.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO REPLY

          To the extent required, ATC respectfully requests leave to submit this Reply. The

Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure prohibit answers to protests unless otherwise

authorized. 21 The Commission regularly allows answers for good cause shown, such as when

the answers help ensure a more accurate and complete record, clarify the issues, or provide

useful and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its deliberative process. 22

ATC’s Reply will clarify the record, correct misinformation and ensure a more accurate and

complete record. Because this information will assist the Commission in its decision-making,

ATC respectfully requests that the Commission accept this Reply for good cause shown.

                                                      8
 III.      CONCLUSION

          For the foregoing reasons, ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC are just

and reasonable and will provide greater clarity and transparency for the immediate and reliable

interconnection of large loads in ATC’s footprint. ATC respectfully requests that the

Commission grant leave to accept this Reply and accept the proposed revisions to Attachment

FF-ATCLLC as just and reasonable, effective October 17, 2026.
